title: The Medallion
full_review:
�
����������� A Hong Kong police detective, endowed by a sacred amulet with superhuman powers, must face down a madman, bent on using the talisman and its young guardian for his own evil designs in the mindless martial-arts comedy "The Medallion" (TriStar).

Director Gordan Chan takes aim at audiences' adrenal glands and funny bones, miserably missing his mark on both with this kung-fu clunker. Even when taking into account the film's lighten-up-it's-only-an-action-film stance, viewing it is akin to watching landfill, with the projector dumping just enough garbage to fill 90 minutes of screen time.

At the risk of wasting too much ink, Jackie Chan stars as Eddie Yang, a cop on the trail of a nefarious international kingpin known only as Snakehead (Julian Sands). At the same time, Snakehead -- or did they mean bonehead -- is relentlessly searching for an oracular holy child, who, as custodian of the eponymous magical medallion, can grant him immortality, always a plus when you're in the global crime business.

Snakehead finds the boy holed up in a backroom Buddhist temple, only to be stymied by Yang. Why the child and powerful artifact are left relatively unguarded in downtown Hong Kong is never explained. Even more inexplicable is why Yang leaves the child unattended, making him easy pickings for Snakehead's goons.

During a successful rescue operation Yang is killed by Snakehead's minions. No worries, the film -- unfortunately -- has several reels left. Using the medallion, the child brings Yang back to life, only now he can run fast and leap up walls -- basically what pre-resurrection Jackie Chan was doing all along, only faster.

The remainder of this abysmal rip-off of Eddie Murphy's 1986 "The Golden Child" plummets from B-movie status through the alphabet, using its threadbare plot of Yang chasing Snakehead chasing Yang for no other reason than to showcase its increasingly tedious action sequences, leading to a chopsocky, crouching-tiger-hidden-story-line climax.

Along the way, Yang is aided by two Interpol agents, the buffoonish Rowan Atkinson-like Arthur Watson (Lee Evans) and the beautiful Nicole James (Claire Forlani), whose performance reeks of an I-needed-the-money career concession.

Perhaps Interpol should have spent less time tracking international loons and allocated more manpower for uncovering the point of this film. The only thing keeping this sinking-quickly-to-video wreck afloat is Chan's buoyant humor and irrefutable athletic prowess, as exhibited in the amazing physical feats peppered throughout, which prove to be the only things worth staying awake for.

Many of the martial-arts sequences employ the now old-hat, wire-flying effects pioneered in Hong Kong action films. Unfortunately, what was elevated to Mona Lisa-grade art in Ang Lee's "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon" has, in Gordan Chan's inept hands, been reduced to the cinematic equivalent of a framed velvet Elvis.

Despite its comic-book context, the film's treatment of violence as the punch line of a joke may give parents pause, as may several scenes which rely on crude toilet humor and double entendre to elicit forced yuks. And while "irreverence" may be overstating the case, the film's lighthearted use of Buddhist religious imagery should irk viewers of all faiths.

Due to action violence and some crass humor and double entendres, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
